content: Patients with primary nephrotic syndrome often require immunosuppressive therapy to achieve remission. However, many patients either experience relapse after undergoing immunosuppressive treatment or exhibit resistance to it. Additionally, immunosuppressive therapy is associated with an increased risk of adverse effects. In China, Huangqi and Huangqi-based formulations have been used for years to treat nephrotic syndrome, but their efficacy and safety have not been systematically evaluated. This review is an update of a previous review first published in 2008. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and potential harms of Huangqi and Huangqi-based formulations in the treatment of nephrotic syndrome across all age groups. These formulations were assessed both as standalone treatments and as adjuncts to other drug therapies. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Chinese Biomedicine Database (CBM), CNKI, and VIP, as well as reference lists of articles. The search was not restricted by language and was last updated in April 2011. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the use of Huangqi or Huangqi-based formulations in treating nephrotic syndrome in both adults and children. These formulations were studied either as sole treatments or in combination with other therapies. Two authors independently assessed the quality of the studies and extracted data. Dichotomous outcomes were reported as relative risks (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), while continuous outcomes were expressed as mean differences (MD) with 95% CI. Nine studies were included in the review. One study was deemed to have a high risk of bias in terms of random sequence generation, while the remaining studies were judged to have a low risk of bias in this area. However, all studies were found to have a high risk of bias for allocation concealment and performance bias. Detection bias was unclear in all studies, while attrition bias was considered low. Two studies had unclear reporting bias, while the rest had low reporting bias. No other significant threats to validity were identified. Huangqi-based formulations demonstrated positive effects compared to control interventions. These included an increase in plasma albumin levels (MD 6.41 g/dL, 95% CI 4.24 to 8.59), a reduction in urine albumin excretion (-0.57 g/24 h, 95% CI -1.04 to -0.10), a decrease in blood cholesterol levels (MD -1.70 mmol/L, 95% CI -2.60 to -1.13), and a reduction in triglyceride levels (-0.33 mmol/L, 95% CI -0.63 to -0.03). Additionally, more patients showed improvement at three months (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.84). However, there was no significant difference between Huangqi-based formulations and control interventions in achieving complete remission (RR 1.59, 95% CI 0.29 to 8.65) or partial remission (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.57 to 2.58). While some formulations showed improvements in the number of patients achieving complete or partial remission, the number of studies evaluating each formulation was small, and the sample sizes ranged from 38 to 78 participants. Relapse rates were reported at varying time points, ranging from three months to three years, making it impossible to pool these results. Complications of nephrotic syndrome and adverse events were reported in only two studies. One study reported complications such as infections, while another study reported adverse reactions to treatment, including Cushing's syndrome, steroid withdrawal syndrome, respiratory tract infections, and upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Both studies indicated that patients treated with Huangqi-based formulations experienced significantly fewer complications or adverse reactions. In conclusion, Huangqi and Huangqi-based formulations may have beneficial effects in the treatment of nephrotic syndrome. These benefits include increased plasma albumin levels, reduced urine albumin excretion, lower blood cholesterol and triglyceride levels, and a decrease in the number of patients who fail to show improvement at three months. Some formulations also showed an increase in the number of patients achieving complete or partial remission. However, the small number of studies and participants limits the strength of these findings.
